Allah here swears by a squadron of horsemen. Each of their military movements is brought forward in sequence: when this squadron begins its attack and advances at great speed towards its destination, the horses snort as they go forward. They strike sparks from the stones with their hooves. Then, right at dawn, they fall upon the enemy; this attack is carried out with extreme swiftness and is sudden. At the moment of the attack, dust rises from the stampede of the horses, because the enemy is not prepared for the assault and its movements are disorganised. When this squadron unexpectedly breaks into the enemy's ranks, severe confusion and agitation break out.

These are the successive steps of a raid that the Arabs knew well. To swear by such a squadron and by the movements of the horses means that such battles are very beloved in Islam; they are beloved to Allah as well, Allah looks upon such actions with favour, and these are praiseworthy values.

Further, these scenes and military actions are more fitting to the meanings upon which the oath is sworn here, as we have clarified in the commentary. The meaning and sense upon which the oath is being sworn is this: it is a psychological disease of man, and it afflicts a person when his psyche is empty of faith. The Qur'an repeatedly points to this reality so that people may struggle against it, because Allah knew how deeply this disease takes root within the human psyche, and how many effects it has upon human personality.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 100, verses 6–8:

Indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord, and he himself bears witness to it, and he is intensely attached to wealth. (100:6–8) "Indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord, and he himself bears witness to it, and he is intensely attached to wealth."

Undoubtedly, man is ungrateful for the blessings of his Lord and practically denies the grace and bounty of Allah. This ingratitude and denial of blessings appears in many forms: in his deeds and in his words. Thus his deeds and words themselves bear witness to this crime of his. It is as if the sun's own light is the proof of the sun (گویا آفتاب آمد دلیل آفتاب): he becomes a witness against himself, and on the Day of Resurrection it will be the same.

"And indeed he is a witness to it" (100:7). And there will come a day when he will give testimony to the truth against himself, about which there is no doubt or dispute.

"And indeed he is intensely attached to wealth" (100:8). He holds his own self and his own interest very dear. Therefore he has a great love for wealth. Wealth is here expressed as "khayr" (good), because man thinks that his welfare lies in property, possessions, power and government, which are the equipment of this world.

This is the nature of man, this is his temperament, and it can change only when faith enters his temperament and his psychology. Through faith his concepts, his values and his standards themselves change. His priorities change. When faith enters his psychology, then denial and ingratitude turn into acknowledgment and thankfulness for Allah's grace. Whereas miserliness and love of wealth are replaced by selflessness and love. Faith gives man values for which he strives, competes and struggles, not greed, avarice, or covetousness. And these values are higher than wealth, power and government, and superior to all worldly and animal values.

The truth is that without faith man is extremely small and petty: his hopes are petty, his priorities are petty, and his aims are petty, even though they may outwardly appear very great. As a person's greed and avarice increase, and as his covetousness becomes intense, his aims may rise, yet he sinks deeper into the mire of earthly values. All his activities are for this life. He becomes confined and imprisoned within his own self, and his liberation from this confinement can be achieved only when he becomes connected with a greater world beyond this world, one that is far higher and distant from it, and far vaster than his own limited world. That is a world created by the Eternal Allah, in which all matters return to the Eternal and Everlasting Allah, and in which the boundaries of this limited world meet a vast and imperishable world.

Thus the final glimpse of the surah is concerned with this, so that the disease of ingratitude and denial may be cured, so that the sickness of selfishness and self-interest may be treated, and so that the fortress of self-worship may be broken and the true human being freed from it. Thus the scene of gathering and resurrection is presented in such a way that man, out of fear, forgets this worldly worship and selfishness, and awakens from the deep sleep of heedlessness and becomes alert.

This is a vivid and forceful scene. For the raising of people from their graves, the intense word "bu'thira" (scattered/overturned, from ba'thara) is used, and in this scene the secrets that human souls had pressed down and kept hidden are being dragged out one by one. The word "hussilat" is used for this, as if government officials were forcibly extracting them. It is as though the tax collectors of the state have arrived, and it is a scene of intense seizing and apprehension.

Does man not know that he must pass through this kind of scene? Does he remember these realities? These realities are in the nature of every human being. If he has this knowledge and remembers it, then this alone is sufficient for his reform. The question is not answered: what would have happened if he had known? Consider it yourselves: what would have happened? A great deal would have happened. If man knew this, very great results would have emerged from this knowledge alone. All these movements and these glimpses end in a final tranquility and rest, on reaching which every movement and every word arrives at its proper place.

All of mankind will return to their Lord, and on that Day Allah will be fully aware of their affairs, their secrets and their circumstances. There is no restriction of that Day; Allah is aware of these circumstances at all times and on every day. But here the word "Yawma'idhin" (on that day) is extremely effective, and its effects make a person alert about that Day. The meaning that on that day Allah will be aware, that is, no one will be able to escape punishment. The reckoning and accounting will be based on complete knowledge and awareness. This implied meaning is what is important here. In short, this entire surah is one continuous scene: a frightening and awe-inspiring scene. Meaning, words and style all change, and this scene comes to its conclusion. This is a particular aspect of the miraculous style of the Quran.
